title: Present tense, -er verbs
goal: By the end of this lesson you can conjugate any regular -er verb in the present tense, know which forms sound the same, and recognise the casual Quebec 'j'parle, j'travaille'.

body: About 90% of French verbs end in *-er* in the infinitive: *parler* (to speak), *aimer* (to like), *habiter* (to live), *travailler* (to work). Almost all of them follow the same pattern, so once you know one, you know thousands.
To conjugate: remove *-er* to get the stem (*parl-*), then add the endings *-e, -es, -e, -ons, -ez, -ent*.
learn.tip: The French present covers English 'I speak', 'I'm speaking' and 'I do speak'.

learn.h: Four forms sound exactly the same
body: The endings *-e, -es, -e* and *-ent* are all silent. *je parle, tu parles, il parle, ils parlent* all sound like [parl]. Only *nous parlons* [par-LÕ] and *vous parlez* [par-LAY] sound different.
This is good news for speaking: you mostly say [parl]. In writing, the endings matter. Never pronounce the *-ent* of *ils parlent*.
learn.tip: ils parlent = eel PARL. The -ent is silent on verbs.

body: Before a verb starting with a vowel or silent h, *je* becomes *j'*: *j'aime, j'habite, j'écoute*. In the plural, liaison links the pronoun: *nous‿aimons, vous‿habitez, ils‿écoutent* [z].
Two small spelling changes: verbs in *-ger* keep an *e* in the nous form (*nous mangeons*), and verbs in *-cer* take a *ç* (*nous commençons*). This keeps the soft g and c sounds.

body: Start with these high-frequency verbs: *parler, aimer, habiter, travailler, manger, regarder* (to watch), *écouter* (to listen to), *chercher* (to look for), *jouer* (to play), *étudier* (to study), *arriver* (to arrive), *rester* (to stay).
Note: *regarder*, *écouter* and *chercher* take a direct object, with no 'at / to / for': *Je regarde la télé. J'écoute la radio. Je cherche mes clés.*

In casual speech everywhere, and very strongly in Quebec, the *e* of *je* drops before a consonant: *je parle* → *j'parle*, *je travaille* → *j'travaille*. Before p, t, k, f and s it can even sound like 'ch': *j'pense* sounds like 'ch'pense'.
Quebec also has handy -er verbs of its own: *magasiner* (to go shopping), *jaser* (to chat), *clavarder* (to chat online). They conjugate like *parler*.

quebec.intro: In casual Quebec speech, je loses its vowel before most verbs: j'parle, j'travaille, j'mange. Quebec also has its own everyday -er verbs like magasiner and jaser.

items.note: magasiner is standard in Quebec, not slang

drills.q: Which form does NOT sound like [parl]?

drills.why: One present tense for 'play' and 'are playing'.

vocab.ex: Le cours commence à neuf heures.

pron.tip: par-LÕ: the only form with a nasal ending.

dialogue.fr: Oui, je commence aujourd'hui. Je m'appelle Nadia.
dialogue.en: Yes, I start today. My name is Nadia.
Welcome! Do you live near here?

dialogue.fr: Non, j'habite à Longueuil. Et toi?
dialogue.en: No, I live in Longueuil. And you?

dialogue.fr: Moi, j'reste à côté. On mange ensemble à midi?
dialogue.en: I live next door. Shall we eat together at noon?

dialogue.fr: Parfait. Après, on magasine un peu?
dialogue.en: Perfect. After, shall we shop a little?

questions.q: When does Nadia start the job?
What do they plan for noon?

speak.prompt: Say where you live, where you work, and what languages you speak.
speak.model: J'habite à Montréal. Je travaille à Laval. Je parle anglais et un peu français.

speak.prompt: Say three things you like and what you watch in the evening.
speak.model: J'aime le café, la musique et le hockey. Je regarde la télé le soir.

speak.prompt: Conjugate 'parler' aloud, then say 'je parle' and 'je pense' the casual Quebec way.
speak.model: je parle, tu parles, il parle, nous parlons, vous parlez, ils parlent. / J'parle, j'pense.

write.prompt: Write 5–6 sentences about a typical weekday using at least five different -er verbs.
write.model: Je travaille à Montréal. Je commence à neuf heures. À midi, je mange avec une collègue. On jase un peu. Le soir, je regarde la télé ou j'écoute de la musique.

quiz.q: What are the present tense endings of -er verbs?
quiz.why: je parle, tu parles, il parle, nous parlons, vous parlez, ils parlent.
-ent is silent: same as il joue.

quiz.why: Without ç, co would sound like 'ko'.
French has one present tense for both.

quiz.q: In casual Quebec, 'je travaille' often sounds like…
quiz.why: The e of je drops; before t it sounds like ch.
